answer.label: Not Gautama Buddha — a modern saying, earliest credited to Frank Outlaw
answer.authorDates: American supermarket executive, president of Bi-Lo Stores · d. 1977
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence the Buddha ever said this, and it appears nowhere in the Pali canon. As Quote Investigator ↗ documents, the earliest close match appeared in a May 1977 San Antonio Light column crediting Frank Outlaw, late president of the Bi-Lo grocery chain — and even that sits atop older 19th-century Christian “sow an act, reap a habit” precursors, so Outlaw is best read as the earliest documented ascription rather than a proven author.

source.excerpt: Watch your thoughts, they become words; watch your words, they become actions; watch your actions, they become habits; watch your habits, they become character; watch your character, it becomes your destiny.
trail: The earliest close match is a May 1977 San Antonio Light column crediting Frank Outlaw of Bi-Lo Stores, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The thought–word–deed–habit–character–destiny chain has 19th-century Christian precursors (an 1856 Essex Standard “sow an act…reap a destiny”), not Buddhist ones, as Quote Investigator ↗ shows.
The Fake Buddha Quotes ↗ project confirms the line is absent from the Dhammapada and the wider Pali canon.
source.excerptNote: The 1977 wording ran with “watch your character, for it becomes your destiny” — the modern form circulates in many near-identical variants.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an evolved popular saying, not a passage from any Buddhist text. Its earliest documented appearance is a 1977 newspaper column ascribing it to Frank Outlaw, but Quote Investigator shows the formula descends from 19th-century Christian precursors, so no single author or first-publication can be fixed with confidence — hence no public-domain claim is asserted here.

author.name: Frank Outlaw
author.heading: Who was Frank Outlaw?
author.metaLine: d. 1977 · American grocer, president of the Bi-Lo supermarket chain
author.bio: Frank Outlaw was an American supermarket executive who led the Bi-Lo Stores chain. He is named as the source of this “watch your thoughts” saying in a May 1977 San Antonio Light newspaper feature published around the time of his death — the earliest known appearance of the modern wording. Whether Outlaw actually coined it or simply repeated an already-circulating maxim is unknown; the underlying thought-to-destiny chain predates him by more than a century.

misattribution.heading: A magnet quote with many false fathers
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely mis-credited sayings on the internet. The same lines get pinned on whichever wise name suits the poster — but the documentary trail points to a 20th-century American grocer and older anonymous sermon material, not any ancient sage.

items.why: The line appears nowhere in the Dhammapada or the wider Pali canon; the Fake Buddha Quotes ↗ project traces the sequence to 19th-century Christian, not Buddhist, sources.
The Lao Tzu credit surfaces only recently (a Goodreads listing dated January 2010) with no Tao Te Ching basis, per Quote Investigator ↗.
An Emerson ascription appears in a 2009 education book with no historical support in Emerson’s writings, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The 2011 film The Iron Lady puts the saying in the mouth of Thatcher’s father, spreading yet another attribution, as Quote Investigator ↗ notes.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented version is a May 1977 San Antonio Light column crediting grocer Frank Outlaw — itself built on anonymous 19th-century “sow an act, reap a destiny” material, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why the saying sticks
lead: The appeal is its staircase logic: each rung — thought, word, action, habit, character, destiny — hands off to the next, turning a moral commonplace into something that feels like a discovered law. That memorable structure is exactly why it drifts so easily onto famous names: attach it to the Buddha or Lao Tzu and the aphorism borrows their authority.

In reality the chain is a Victorian sermon device. Nineteenth-century Christian writers used the “sow an act, reap a habit…reap a destiny” progression to teach character-building, and the modern “watch your…” phrasing crystallized only in the 1970s.
context.pull: A Victorian pulpit device, re-pinned on the Buddha.
